name: ABL Landscape Architecture
description: ABL Landscape Architecture is an award-winning, client-focused landscape architecture firm based in Lexington, Virginia offering expertise in institutional, civic, residential and commercial landscape architecture projects.
statement: ABL Landscape Architecture is principally devoted to the adaptation of historic, environmentally sensitive landscapes to contemporary needs and goals.

intro: The firm seeks to distill the essence of a site, and to respond to its innate character and context with creative, enduring design. ABL assists clients through all phases from initial concept to landscape establishment and maturation. We embrace open dialogue and exploration with clients, allied professionals, contractors, and end-users.

Mindful of the client's need to visualize the final product and also of the client's cost constraints in landscape construction and maintenance, ABL seeks every reasonable means to narrow the uncertainty between design incubation and the desired outcome. Such techniques include photo simulation, 3D scale models, material samples, full scale mock-ups, detailed review of pricing, dialogue with both grounds staff and end-users, and frequent site visits.
studio.note: ABL is a SWaM certified small business.

process.lead: We are three people, and we do the work ourselves. A project begins with a meeting, at which the client tells us what they want of a place; from there we research the site, draw it, and return to it through construction, until the planting has taken hold.
intro: Our work ranges from private gardens to the Virginia Horse Center and the campuses of Washington and Lee University and the Virginia Military Institute. Before founding ABL, Arthur Bartenstein practiced with Peter Walker and Partners and the SWA Group in California and with Hill Studio in Roanoke and Frazier Associates in Staunton, on projects in Florida, California, Northern Virginia, Japan and China.

sections.title: Research
text: Before we draw anything we learn the history of the ground: how the site came to be as it is, what it was made for, and what has been done to it since. At Courthouse Square in Lexington that history starts with the act of 1777, which set the county court on the first Tuesday of each month. Court Day brought families in from the outlying farms to trade and to hear the news, and the square was where they gathered. From this we took the premise of the design, that the square is first a place of assembly; the level terraces, the ramps and the benches follow from it.

In Lexington and Rockbridge County we come to a project with much of this history in hand. Arthur Bartenstein is president of the Rockbridge Historical Society and serves on the City of Lexington's Architectural Review Board and Tree Committee.

quote.text: Registered in terms of place, but also registered in terms of time.
quote.by: Arthur Bartenstein, on what the firm's work should be

sections.title: Dialogue
text: Arthur Bartenstein's diagram of the work is a triangle, with the client, the site and the design team at its corners and arrows running both ways along its sides. The client tells us what is wanted; the site tests the idea and dictates part of the answer; and the conversation among the three continues until the design is settled. On a campus or a civic project it takes in the architect, the engineers and the staff who will maintain the grounds, and we bring them the design while it can still change.

sections.title: Mock-ups
text: A client is asked to approve a place that does not yet exist, and to pay for it. So we show the design in every way we can before it is built: in sketches, photo simulations and scale models, in samples of the materials, and, before construction begins, in a mock-up at full scale on the site itself. We review the pricing in the same detail, including what the place will cost to maintain.

quote.text: The secret to getting good work.
quote.by: Arthur Bartenstein, on the full-scale mock-up

sections.title: Construction and after
text: We stay with a project while it is built and afterward, until the planting is established. We have worked with many of the county's contractors for decades, and we are on the site often while the work goes in. Kelly Morikawa, a certified arborist, owned and operated a landscape design, installation and maintenance company here for eighteen years, and she and Bugs Utsey know which plants do well in this ground.

services.intro: For a house, a garden or a farm, people come to us for one of four things.

items.name: Consultation
items.text: We visit the property and say what we would do with it.

items.name: Planting plan
items.text: Kelly Morikawa and Bugs Utsey draw a plan of what to plant and where.

items.name: Master plan
items.text: A design for the whole property, carried from research through drawings a contractor can build from and our visits to the site during construction.

items.name: A single element
items.text: One part of a property, a stair for example, designed and seen through construction.

services.outro: Each takes research, and anything that is to be built is mocked up first.
